presentingComplaint: Fever, productive cough with foul-smelling sputum and breathlessness for 4 days
history: 71-year-old man brought in by family with 4 days of fever, cough productive of copious foul-smelling sputum, and progressive breathlessness. He had an ischaemic stroke 8 months ago leaving him with dysphagia and occasional coughing episodes during meals; the family describes recurrent choking on thin liquids. He is bed-bound much of the day. Background of hypertension and heavy alcohol use. No recent hospitalisation or antibiotics. Onset was subacute over days rather than hours.
examination: Ill-appearing, mildly confused elderly man. Poor dentition with gingival disease. Reduced gag reflex noted. Bronchial breathing and coarse crepitations over the right lower and mid zones (gravity-dependent segments), with dullness to percussion. No neck stiffness. No calf swelling; chest wall non-tender. No peripheral stigmata of endocarditis.
imaging: Chest radiograph: consolidation in the right lower lobe and posterior segment of right upper lobe (gravity-dependent zones typical of aspiration in a recumbent/supine patient); no discrete cavity or air-fluid level at this stage; small associated right pleural reaction.
microbiology: Sputum Gram stain: mixed flora with polymorphs; blood cultures sent, pending. Sputum culture pending (anaerobes and oral streptococci suspected).
citations: Harrison 22e — Pneumonia (Aspiration and Anaerobic Pulmonary Infections)
stewardship: Empiric ampicillin-sulbactam IV (covers oral streptococci, anaerobes and enteric Gram-negatives) as guideline-concordant choice for aspiration pneumonia with dependency on anaerobic/oral-flora coverage; amoxicillin-clavulanate is an oral step-down. Reserve routine anaerobic coverage for suspected abscess/empyema per 2019 IDSA/ATS guidance, but the foul sputum, dental disease and dependent-lobe consolidation here justify it. Address the underlying dysphagia (swallow assessment) to prevent recurrence.
contraindications: Penicillin allergy — substitute a respiratory fluoroquinolone (moxifloxacin) or clindamycin for anaerobic cover
Avoid nephrotoxic combinations; monitor renal function given age and alcohol use
Clindamycin carries a higher C. difficile risk
edgeCases: Chemical (Mendelson) aspiration pneumonitis can mimic infection early but is sterile and often improves in 24-48h without antibiotics — avoid overtreatment
Progression to lung abscess/empyema with cavitation and air-fluid level if untreated, especially with poor dentition and anaerobes
expectedMaiK: Classic aspiration pneumonia in an elderly post-stroke patient with dysphagia: consolidation in gravity-dependent lung segments with foul sputum points to oral/anaerobic flora. Treat with ampicillin-sulbactam and arrange a swallow assessment to prevent recurrence.
expectedNextQuestions: Is there a witnessed aspiration or documented dysphagia / abnormal swallow, and what is the level of consciousness?
Any poor dentition, periodontal disease, or reduced gag reflex?
expectedInvestigations: Chest radiograph (and CT chest if abscess/empyema suspected)
Bedside swallow evaluation / formal SALT assessment
regressionAssertions: empiric regimen must include anaerobic/oral-flora coverage (ampicillin-sulbactam or amoxicillin-clavulanate)
